issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a Stock class (with methods add, take, findStockIngredient, addToStockIngredients, emptyStock) and instruct SealSaloon.stock to be of type Stock, but the template repository provides an Inventory class that implements those methods while Stock.java in the template is empty. The solution also uses Inventory (SealSaloon declares a static Inventory stock). This class-name/type mismatch (Stock vs Inventory) is a structural inconsistency that will confuse students about which class to implement or modify and may block them from following the specification.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the class name consistent across artifacts. Either rename Inventory to Stock in the template and solution (move Inventory implementation into Stock.java and remove the empty Stock file) and update references accordingly, or update the problem statement and UML to refer to Inventory instead of Stock. Ensure SealSaloon.stock uses the same class type declared in the template and UML so students clearly know which class to implement/modify.

issues.description: The problem statement consistently refers to a class named 'Stock' (including UML and requirements that SealSaloon.stock be a final/static Stock), but the provided template and the solution repository implement and use a class named 'Inventory' with the exact methods and behavior expected of 'Stock'. Additionally, Stock.java in both repositories is empty. This name mismatch (Stock vs Inventory) refers to the same conceptual entity (the saloon's shared ingredient storage) and will confuse students who look for a 'Stock' implementation mentioned in the problem but find 'Inventory' in the codebase.
issues.suggestedFix: Unify the identifier for the shared ingredient storage across all artifacts. Recommended fix: rename the Inventory class and file (Inventory.java, class Inventory) to Stock (Stock.java, class Stock) in the template and solution, and update all references (e.g., SealSaloon.stock type) accordingly. Alternatively, update the problem statement to refer to 'Inventory' instead of 'Stock' — but prefer renaming code to 'Stock' to match the problem description and UML.
